2027-06-22.title: Tuesday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time · St Paulinus of Nola; Sts John Fisher and Thomas More
readings: Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred
He who does justice will live in the presence of the Lord
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you
2027-06-22.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). Two optional memorials may be kept: St Paulinus of Nola, bishop; and Sts John Fisher, bishop, and Thomas More, martyrs. Liturgical colour: green (white if St Paulinus is remembered, red for the martyrs).
2027-06-22.verse: Then Abram said to Lot, “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.”
theo: Abram has come back from Egypt a rich man: “Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.” His nephew Lot has also grown rich, with “flocks and herds and tents.” And riches bring their usual trouble: “the land could not support both of them living together,” and “there was strife between the herders of Abram's livestock and the herders of Lot's livestock.” Every Kerala family that has quarrelled over a boundary wall, a coconut tree on the dividing line or the share of an ancestral house will recognise the scene. Abram is the elder and the head of the clan; by custom the choice is his. But he speaks first for peace: “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.” And then he does something astonishing: he gives the choice to the younger man. “Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left.” Lot looks and sees with the eyes of the market: the plain of the Jordan, “well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD.” He chooses it, and moves his tent “as far as Sodom.” The narrator adds a quiet warning: “Now the people of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.” What looks best to the eye is not always best for the soul. Then, when Lot has gone, God speaks to Abram, who has kept the poorer hill country: “Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.” The man who let go receives everything. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and, as always, builds an altar. The Psalm draws the portrait of such a man: “Those who walk blamelessly, and do what is right, and speak the truth from their heart,” who “stand by their oath even to their hurt” and “do not take a bribe against the innocent.” “Those who do these things shall never be moved.”

The Gospel gathers three sayings from the end of the Sermon on the Mount. The first is about reverence: “Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine.” Holy things must be treated as holy; the early Christians applied this word to the Eucharist, which, as the Didache says, is only for the baptised. The second is the saying the world calls the Golden Rule: “In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.” Jewish teachers before Jesus had taught the same wisdom in its negative form, do not do to others what you hate (Tobit 4:15); Jesus puts it positively, and so turns it from a limit into a programme: do not only avoid harming, but go and do the good you would hope for. Abram did exactly this with Lot. The third saying is the hardest: “Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the road is easy that leads to destruction, and there are many who take it. For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it.” Today's optional memorials show three men who found the narrow gate. St Paulinus of Nola, a rich Roman senator and governor in the fourth century, was baptised, and with his wife Therasia gave away his great wealth to the poor; he settled at Nola near Naples beside the shrine of the martyr St Felix, became a priest and then bishop, and wrote Christian poetry and letters to friends such as Augustine and Jerome. St John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, and St Thomas More, Lord Chancellor of England, were the two most respected men of their country when King Henry VIII demanded an oath that went against their conscience and their communion with the Pope. Under great pressure, almost everyone swore. They stood by the truth “even to their hurt.” Fisher was beheaded on 22 June 1535, More on 6 July. More is reported to have said on the scaffold that he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
outline: Ask: has a quarrel over land, property or inheritance ever divided your family?
Point 1 · No strife, for we are kindred
Abram chooses peace over property and gives Lot the first choice.
The one who lets go receives from God; Lot's eyes lead him toward Sodom.
Point 3 · The golden rule and the narrow gate
Do to others what you would want, and walk the narrow road, like Fisher and More.
“Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred.”
live: If there is a quarrel in your family or neighbourhood over land, money or an inheritance, take one step toward peace this week, even at some cost to yourself.
Before speaking to or about anyone today, ask: how would I want to be spoken to or about? Then do that.
saints: Born near Bordeaux of a wealthy Roman family, he became a senator and governor of Campania. Baptised around 389, he and his wife Therasia sold their estates for the poor. He was ordained priest and settled at Nola near Naples beside the tomb of the martyr St Felix, where he cared for pilgrims and the poor; about 409 he became bishop of Nola. A gifted poet, he corresponded with Sts Augustine, Jerome and Martin of Tours.
Sts John Fisher (1469–1535) and Thomas More (1478–1535)

John Fisher, bishop of Rochester and chancellor of the University of Cambridge, was a scholar and a devoted pastor. Thomas More, lawyer, writer and father of a large household, became Lord Chancellor of England. Both refused to take the oath required by King Henry VIII that rejected the authority of the Pope over the Church in England. Fisher, created a cardinal while in prison, was beheaded on 22 June 1535; More on 6 July 1535. They were canonised by Pius XI in 1935; in 2000 St John Paul II named Thomas More patron of statesmen and politicians.
2027-06-22.prayer: O God, who in martyrdom have brought true faith to its highest expression, graciously grant that, strengthened through the intercession of Saint John Fisher and Saint Thomas More, we may confirm by the witness of our life the faith we profess with our lips. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, you blessed Abram when he chose peace with his kinsman over the best land. Heal the quarrels in our families over property and inheritance; teach us to do to others as we would have them do to us; and give us courage, like St Paulinus, St John Fisher and St Thomas More, to enter through the narrow gate that leads to life. Amen.
altar: Before Communion the priest prays: Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles, peace I leave you, my peace I give you, look not on our sins but on the faith of your Church, and graciously grant her peace and unity. Then we offer one another a sign of peace. Like Abram with Lot, we may not come to the altar holding on to strife with our kin; the Lord who gives himself to us asks us first to be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24).

quick: When strife arises between their herders, Abram chooses peace with Lot, saying: we are kindred, and gives the younger man the first choice of land.
Lot chooses the well-watered plain toward Sodom; God then promises Abram all the land he can see and offspring like the dust of the earth.
Jesus teaches: do not give what is holy to dogs; do to others as you would have them do to you; enter through the narrow gate.
2027-06-22.action: Take one step toward peace in a family or neighbourhood quarrel, even at some cost to yourself.
2027-06-22.question: Do I care more about my share than about peace with my brothers and sisters?
kidsaint: John Fisher was a bishop in England about five hundred years ago. He was a very clever teacher at the university, but he also loved the poor people of his diocese and visited them often. When the king ordered everyone to say that the king, and not the Pope, was the head of the Church in England, Bishop John said no, gently but firmly. He was old and sick, but he was put in prison and then put to death. Before he died he read a verse from St John's Gospel: this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God. Lesson: even when everyone else does what is wrong, ask Jesus for courage to do what is right.

family.explain: Abram and his nephew Lot had so many sheep and cows that their shepherds began to fight about the grass. Abram said: let us not fight, we are family! You choose first which land you want. Lot took the best land, but God gave Abram an even bigger blessing. Jesus said: do to others what you would like them to do to you.
family.intention: We pray for families who are quarrelling about land or money, that they may make peace.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone in our family or among our neighbours we should make peace with? What can we do first?”

illus: Two brothers in a village near Pala had not spoken for eleven years because of a dispute over three cents of land and a well on the boundary. The case went from one court to another, and the lawyers' fees were greater than the price of the land. One Sunday the elder brother heard Genesis 13 read at Mass and could not sleep that night. The next morning he walked to his brother's house, which he had not entered in eleven years, and said: take the well and the land; I want my brother back. The younger brother withdrew the case the same week. Their families now share the well. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are our peace. Heal our quarrels, teach us your golden rule, and give us courage for the narrow way. Amen.
share: Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred (Genesis 13:8). Where is there strife in my family or community that I could help to heal?
Raise your eyes now, and look (Genesis 13:14). When I gave something up for peace, how did God bless me?
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12). How would my words and actions change if I lived this rule today?
pm.resp: He who does justice will live in the presence of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that her children may be peacemakers in families divided by property and inheritance.
For lawyers, judges and politicians, through the prayers of St Thomas More, that they may serve the common good and keep their conscience clean.
For bishops, through the prayers of St John Fisher and St Paulinus, that they may be faithful shepherds and lovers of the poor.
For Christians who suffer for refusing to act against their conscience.
For our group, that we may choose the narrow gate and practise the golden rule at home.
pm.close: Father, you blessed Abram for choosing peace. Make us peacemakers, and lead us by the narrow road to life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading could have happened in any village in Kerala. Abram and his nephew Lot have become rich, and their herdsmen start fighting over the grass and the water. How many families have been broken by fights over land, a boundary or an inheritance? Brothers who do not speak, cases that go on for twenty years.

Abram, the elder, could have taken the best land for himself. Instead he says: let there be no strife between you and me, for we are kindred (Genesis 13:8). And he lets Lot choose first. Lot chooses the green, well-watered plain, near Sodom. It looks good, but it leads him into trouble. Abram takes what is left. And then God says to him: raise your eyes and look in every direction; all the land that you see I will give to you (Genesis 13:14–15). The one who let go for the sake of peace receives everything from God.

In the Gospel Jesus gives the rule that Abram lived: in everything do to others as you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12). It is simple to say and hard to do. And he warns that the road to life is narrow: the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it (Matthew 7:14).

St John Fisher and St Thomas More, whom we may remember today, chose that narrow gate. When the king demanded an oath against their conscience and against unity with the Pope, almost everyone took it. They refused, and gave their lives. Today, let us ask for their courage, and for Abram's generosity. If there is a quarrel in our family over land or money, let us be the first to say: let there be no strife between us, for we are kindred. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever fought with your brother or sister over a toy, or the best seat, or the biggest piece of cake? Abram and his nephew Lot had a fight between their shepherds. Abram said: let us not fight, we are family. You choose first! Jesus gave us a golden rule: do to others what you would like them to do to you. Today, try to let someone else choose first, and see how happy it makes them, and Jesus.

intro: Theme: “Let there be no strife between you and me, for we are kindred.”
Abram chooses peace over property, God blesses the one who lets go, and Jesus gives the golden rule and the narrow gate.

points.h: No strife, for we are kindred
sub: The elder gives the first choice.
q: Then Abram said to Lot, “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.
If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
points.apply: Be the first to speak a word of peace in a quarrel in your family or neighbourhood this week.

sub: Lot looks with the eyes of the market.
The one who lets go receives.
q: Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
points.apply: Before a big decision this week, ask not only what looks best but what is best for your soul and your family.

points.h: The golden rule and the narrow gate
sub: Few find the narrow road: Fisher and More.
q: O Lord, who may abide in your tent? Who may dwell on your holy hill? Those who walk blamelessly, and do what is right, and speak the truth from their heart;
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.
points.apply: Choose one situation at home or at work this week where you will act by the golden rule even if it costs you.

concl: Abram chose peace with his kinsman over the best land, and God gave him more than he gave up.
Jesus asks us to do to others what we want for ourselves and to walk the narrow road, as Sts John Fisher and Thomas More did.
2027-06-22.resolve: Make peace in one quarrel and practise the golden rule each day this week.
